questions.q: What does the first principal component represent?
options: The direction along which the data varies the most
The single most important original column
The average of all the features
The cluster with the most rows
questions.explain: PC1 is the direction of greatest variance. It is a weighted blend of the original columns, not one of them.

questions.q: Why should you standardize features before PCA?
options: PCA only runs on integer data
Standardizing increases the number of components
PCA maximizes variance, so a column with large units, like annual spend, would dominate
Standardizing removes the need for explained variance
questions.explain: Unscaled features with big numeric ranges have big variance and would dominate the first components.

questions.q: In the lesson, explained variance ratios were [0.485, 0.46, 0.023, 0.016, 0.009, 0.007]. How many components make sense to keep?
options: 2, since together they explain about 94.5 percent and the rest add little
questions.explain: The cumulative variance jumps to 0.945 after two components, then barely moves. That cliff and flat tail is the scree pattern.

options: Keeps the smallest number of components that explains at least 90 percent of the variance
questions.explain: A fraction between 0 and 1 tells scikit-learn to choose the number of components to reach that share of explained variance.

questions.q: What is the main cost of using PCA components as features?
options: PCA can only be used once per project
The components are blends of original columns, so they are harder to explain to stakeholders
PCA always makes models less accurate
questions.explain: PCA yields fewer, uncorrelated features, but a component like 'PC2' is a weighted mix of columns rather than a familiar business measure.
